notes: The Hebrew repeats “Name” and describes the LORD as enthroned above the cherubim. The ark bears his name; it is not identified with God.

The source names cypress wood in verse 5. The instruments and tree identification are uncertain. “Stumbled” describes the oxen’s action; “irreverent act” translates a rare, difficult expression. The text explicitly attributes Uzzah’s death to God.
“Date cake” is an uncertain identification of one of the three gifts; “portion of meat” is another interpretation.
Michal’s accusation of exposure is her speech. Verse 23 states that she had no child, but does not explain why.
vocabulary: Perez-uzzah
The name echoes the LORD’s “breaking out” against Uzzah. Compare the breaking-through language in 5:20.
Ephod
A garment associated with priestly service; here David wears a linen ephod.
LORD of Armies
A divine title also rendered “LORD of Hosts.” The title’s scope is not limited here to a single human army.

sections.1: A House for the LORD, a House for David

notes: The pinned Hebrew says “tribes,” not “judges.” The relationship between the tribes and the command to shepherd is compressed.
“House” moves between a building and a continuing family or dynasty. The promise keeps offspring, name, kingdom, and throne connected. Verse 16 reads “before you.”

The final phrase is difficult: literally, “and this is the instruction/law of humankind.” It can be read as a statement about instruction for humanity or, as here, a question about the human way of proceeding.

The Hebrew shifts between speaking about God and addressing him, and briefly uses a plural “you,” apparently addressing Israel. The English makes these shifts more continuous. The final “nations and their gods” is grammatically compressed; its attachment remains uncertain.
The Hebrew says God “uncovered the ear” of his servant and the servant “found his heart” to pray. The English unfolds these as revelation and courage.
vocabulary: Plant
An image of giving the people a settled place in which to live.
Steadfast love
Committed love that continues through the relationship; the promise explicitly distinguishes discipline from abandonment.
Lord GOD
This form represents the title “Lord” followed by the divine name, here printed GOD.

notes: Metheg-ammah is retained as a name. The expression can also be understood as “the bridle of the mother city”; its exact reference is uncertain.
The read tradition supplies “Euphrates,” absent from the written line. The source gives seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers.
The pinned text says Aram in verse 12 and Arameans in verse 13, followed by Edom in verse 14. The draft preserves the sequence.
The source names Ahimelech son of Abiathar and calls David’s sons “priests.” It does not explain their duties here.
vocabulary: Tribute
Goods paid to an overlord by a subject people.
Hamstrung
Disabled the horses by cutting the tendons of their hind legs.
Justice and righteousness
A paired description of the king’s responsibility to govern rightly.

notes: Saul is called a “father” in the Hebrew kinship idiom; the family context identifies him as Mephibosheth’s grandfather.
The Hebrew abruptly says “my table.” The draft takes this as a return to David’s promise and supplies an introduction. The speaker transition is not explicit in the source.
The chapter repeats both Mephibosheth’s place at the table and his disability. It does not turn his disability into a moral or spiritual condition.
vocabulary: Steadfast love
David’s stated reason for seeking Jonathan’s surviving family.
Dead dog
Mephibosheth’s self-abasing description in his own speech.

notes: The cutting of clothes exposes the men’s buttocks. Their humiliation is not reduced to a change in clothing style.
Joab urges courage but leaves the outcome to what the LORD considers good.
The source gives seven hundred chariot fighters and forty thousand horsemen. These categories and numbers are retained.
vocabulary: A stench
An image of becoming deeply offensive to someone.
The River
Here the Euphrates, the major river associated with the Aramean territories.

sections.14: David Sends Uriah to His Death

notes: David is on the roof. The text does not say where Bathsheba is bathing. It says David sent, took her, and slept with her; it does not report her consent, a seduction, or her thoughts. Her message in verse 5 is quoted directly.
Purification concerns ritual uncleanness, likely connected here with menstruation. Ritual uncleanness is not a claim of moral wrongdoing.
“Wash your feet” remains a homecoming expression in the text. Uriah himself makes the prospect of sleeping with his wife explicit in verse 11.
The source uses Jerubbesheth. The draft retains that form rather than replacing it with Jerubbaal.
David tells Joab not to regard the deaths as evil; the narrator closes by calling David’s action evil in the LORD’s eyes.
vocabulary: Shelters
Temporary dwellings, also called booths; Uriah contrasts them with his own home.
Upper millstone
The upper stone used to grind grain against a lower stone.
The sword devours
An image of killing used here in David’s attempt to reassure Joab.

notes: The read form has “my eyes”; the written form has “his eyes.” The accusation holds David responsible for killing Uriah through the Ammonites.
The announced harm includes David’s wives being taken and sexual access made public. The women’s consent is not stated.

The pinned Hebrew says David has treated “the enemies of the LORD” with contempt. This is difficult in context. It is often understood indirectly as giving those enemies cause for contempt toward the LORD. The draft retains the direct wording and leaves the difficulty visible.
The servants fear he may “do something harmful.” The Hebrew does not specify the person who might be harmed.
“I will go to him” points toward David’s own death. The verse does not describe the conditions of an afterlife.

The read form says that she named Solomon; the written form says he did. The next verse’s subjects are compressed: the draft understands the LORD to send word through Nathan and Nathan to give the name Jedidiah.
“Their king” can also be read as the name of a deity, Milcom. The source states a talent of gold and a precious stone, and says the crown was placed on David’s head.

The instrument language is disputed: it can be understood as brutal execution or as forced labor with saws, iron tools, and brickmaking. The draft keeps the severe “under” and “pass through” language without claiming the method is certain.
vocabulary: Ewe lamb
A young female sheep. The story calls her like a daughter to the poor man.
Jedidiah
“Beloved of the LORD,” connecting the name with the preceding statement of love.
Water city
Probably the part of Rabbah associated with its water supply; the precise layout is not explained.
Talent
A large unit of weight; no modern weight is inserted into the verse.

notes: Tamar refuses, calls the proposed act an outrage, and is overpowered. “Raped” makes the forced intercourse explicit. Her appeal to speak with the king is not a narrator’s ruling that the proposed marriage was permitted.
The robe’s Hebrew expression also occurs in Joseph’s story. Its exact design is uncertain; long sleeves and ornamentation are possible understandings.
Absalom’s instruction to keep quiet is his response, not advice to the reader. Tamar remains desolate. The pinned text reports David’s anger but gives no further action by him here.
The first report says all the sons died; Jonadab corrects it. The narrative preserves the inaccurate report as a report.

The Hebrew construction is incomplete. The draft understands an implied longing to go to Absalom. Another possible sense is that David ceased going out against him. The direction of the king’s heart in 14:1 is also open to interpretation.
vocabulary: Outrage
A disgraceful violation of the community’s moral order.
Be strong and courageous
A familiar encouragement formula placed here in Absalom’s order to kill.

notes: The woman’s story is a performance arranged by Joab. Its threatened destruction of the remaining heir is part of her argument.

The statement about God not taking life is difficult, and belongs to the woman’s persuasive speech. The draft does not expand it into a universal claim that God never judges or that every banishment ends.
Return to Jerusalem does not yet mean access to the king. The repeated prohibition on seeing his face remains.
The source states two hundred shekels of hair by the royal weight, and three sons and one daughter. It does not explain the later statement “I have no son” in 18:18.
vocabulary: Last ember
An image for the surviving son through whom the family’s name could continue.
Avenger of blood
A relative charged with pursuing a killing; the story invokes this role in the threat to the remaining son.
Hand in this
An image of involvement or agency, here identifying Joab’s part.

sections.24: The Ark Returns to the City

notes: The pinned Hebrew says forty years. It does not identify the starting point. This draft retains the number instead of silently replacing it with four.
“The last house” may instead designate a place called Beth-merhak.
Ittai is a foreigner and exile. David offers release from following him; Ittai’s reply is a pledge extending to death.
The source says Abiathar “came up.” It does not explicitly say he offered sacrifices at this point.
“Are you not a seer?” is difficult; it can also be taken as an appeal to see or understand. Verse 28 follows the read “plains”; the written form refers to crossings.
David gives Hushai a proposed profession of allegiance and a route for sending news. Hushai’s actual answer to Absalom is narrated in chapter 16.
vocabulary: Stole the hearts
The narrator’s description of Absalom winning the people’s allegiance.
Cherethites and Pelethites
Named groups serving in David’s guard.
Favor in the LORD’s eyes
David makes his return conditional on the LORD’s favor, not possession of the ark.

notes: Ziba reports Mephibosheth’s alleged words. In chapter 19 Mephibosheth gives a conflicting account. The translation does not settle that dispute by changing either speaker’s claim.

David considers and then asserts a divine role in Shimei’s cursing; these are David’s words. Verse 12’s read form is “my eye,” interpreted here as tears. The written form is “my guilt”; the expression remains uncertain.
Hushai initially leaves the chosen king unnamed. His words retain their possible double meaning.
Absalom’s action uses the women left behind as a public claim against his father. Their consent is not reported. Their later confinement is narrated in 20:3.
vocabulary: Man of blood
Shimei’s accusation of bloodshed or bloodguilt.
Steadfast love
Here the word concerns loyalty between friends.
Strengthened hands
An image of increased resolve among Absalom’s followers.

notes: The middle clause is compressed and difficult. The draft understands bringing the people back to depend on removing David, the single target named in verse 2.
Hushai’s bear, lion, sand, dew, and ropes images are part of his persuasive speech. Verse 14 separately calls Ahithophel’s counsel good and attributes its frustration to the LORD.
The source names Ithra the Israelite and Abigail daughter of Nahash. These are retained without harmonizing another family account.
The list repeats roasted grain. The final herd product is probably cheese or a similar dairy food; its precise identification is uncertain.
vocabulary: Slave woman
The unnamed woman carries the information to the two waiting messengers.
Put his household in order
Ahithophel arranged his affairs before his death.

notes: The pinned text reads “now,” followed by “like us, ten thousand.” Its syntax is uncertain. The familiar “you are worth ten thousand of us” understands or changes the opening as “you.” The draft keeps the difficult reading and flags it for editorial review.
The text says Absalom’s head caught in the tree, not specifically his hair.
The soldier’s report of the protective order is compressed. Verse 13 follows the read “my life,” not the written “his life.” Verse 14 repeats “heart” for Absalom and the tree.
The statement “I have no son” is retained alongside the three sons reported in 14:27. The text does not explain the difference.
The final phrase may mean news that brings no reward, or news without a useful outcome.
This verse is numbered 19:1 in the pinned Hebrew source. The following public chapter 19 is consequently offset by one.
vocabulary: Monument
The Hebrew word is “hand,” used here for a memorial that carries Absalom’s name.
Cushite
A man identified by origin in Cush; no personal name is given.
Well
The word also means peace. The victory greetings lead to David’s repeated question about Absalom’s well-being.

notes: These public verses correspond to Hebrew 19:2–44. No source verse is omitted or duplicated.
The king appeals to kinship and promises Amasa command in Joab’s place. The immediate subject of “he turned the hearts” is not stated by name.
The crossing expression is difficult. It may refer to a crossing party, crossing operation, or ferry.

The narrator reports Mephibosheth’s neglected grooming. His allegation of deception conflicts with Ziba’s report in 16:3. David divides the land without stating which account he accepts. Verse 25 retains “to Jerusalem,” although the surrounding movements make the location difficult.
Chimham’s relationship to Barzillai is not stated here. Verse 40 spells the name Chimhan; the draft preserves that form.
vocabulary: Bone and flesh
A kinship appeal, also used when Israel first approached David in 5:1.
Adversaries
The Hebrew uses satan here for human opponents, the sons of Zeruiah.
Ten shares
Israel’s stated claim to a larger stake in the king than Judah.

notes: The ten women receive provision but remain confined until death. “Living as widows” is the source’s description; it does not make them responsible for what Absalom did.
The sword’s movement is compressed. The text does not explain how it fell from its sheath and came to be in Joab’s hand. The fatal violence is stated explicitly.
The source says Berites; their identity is uncertain. The draft understands Sheba as the unnamed traveler and preserves the difficult sequence of place names.
The woman invokes Abel’s reputation for counsel. Joab’s denial of destruction is his speech. The city is spared through Sheba’s killing, not through a bloodless settlement.
The source calls Ira a priest for David. His precise duties are not specified.
vocabulary: Share and inheritance
The rebellion’s slogan rejects a stake in David’s rule, answering the preceding argument over shares.
A mother in Israel
The city is pictured as a mother; the image emphasizes a community facing destruction.
Forced labor
Compulsory work administered by a royal official.

notes: The LORD’s answer identifies bloodguilt. The demand for seven descendants comes from the Gibeonites, and David agrees to it. The passage does not quote a divine command prescribing their execution.
The verb refers to lethal public exposure, often understood as hanging or impalement. The precise method is uncertain; the deaths are explicit.

Two different men are named Mephibosheth: Jonathan’s son is spared; Rizpah’s son is handed over. Verse 8 reads Michal and says she bore five sons. This conflicts with other family notices, including 6:23. The draft does not silently substitute Merab or “raised.”
Rizpah guards the bodies until rain falls. David then retrieves and gathers remains for burial. The answered pleas for the land are reported after these actions.
The pinned text says Elhanan struck down Goliath. It does not say “Goliath’s brother.” The draft preserves this difficulty alongside the earlier David account.
vocabulary: Atonement
Dealing with the offense and its consequences so the relationship can be restored; David asks what will accomplish it here.
Rapha
A name or ancestral designation associated here with unusually formidable warriors.
Israel’s lamp
The men’s image of David’s life and continuing leadership.

notes: The poem retains its own wording and images. Similarity to another biblical song does not authorize replacing this source’s lines. Its violent victories and claims of righteousness remain David’s sung words.
The Hebrew says “he appeared” or “was seen,” not “he soared.”
The speaker claims righteousness, clean hands, and blamelessness. These statements are retained alongside the narrative’s accounts of his wrongdoing.

Verse 33’s verb is difficult; “clears my way completely” retains a sense of release and an unobstructed way. Verses 33–34 follow the read “my way” and “my feet.” In verse 36, “your answering me” is one understanding of a difficult expression also associated with gentleness or condescension.
The verb is unusual. “Come limping” expresses one possible sense; the form is also associated with girding oneself.
The read tradition has “tower of salvation.” The written form can be read as magnifying or giving great victories.
vocabulary: Horn of salvation
A horn is an image of strength; the phrase pictures effective saving power.
Sheol
The realm of the dead, pictured here with cords that entangle.
Refined
An image of metal tested and purified by fire, applied to the LORD’s word.
Anointed
The king designated by anointing, here identified as David with his continuing offspring.

notes: “Sweet singer of Israel’s songs” renders a compressed description that may instead mean the favored one of Israel’s songs. “Last words” need not identify these as his final spoken syllables.

The draft takes the two negative clauses as questions expecting agreement. They can also be read as statements beginning “my house is not so” and “he does not make it spring up.” The covenant language between them is explicit.
The source’s names and syntax are difficult. Josheb-basshebeth, Adino the Eznite, and the eight hundred slain are retained rather than reconstructed as a spear-wielding clause.
The pinned text repeatedly says Three here, even while distinguishing Abishai from the Three. The draft leaves that tension visible instead of silently substituting Thirty.
The Hebrew has “two ariels of Moab.” It does not explicitly include “sons.” The referents are uncertain.

Several roster relationships are compressed, especially the sons of Jashen and the Maacathite entry. The source’s names and final total of thirty-seven are retained without inventing missing persons or deleting entries to force a count.
vocabulary: Declaration
A solemn utterance, also used to introduce prophetic speech.
Everlasting covenant
The enduring commitment that David names in relation to his house.
Ariels
A difficult term that can suggest lionlike champions or be associated with a name or cultic object; the verse does not settle the identification.
The Thirty
A named group of warriors; the title and the final stated total are both retained.

sections.18: An Altar at Araunah’s Threshing Floor

notes: The passage attributes the incitement to the LORD and later records David’s confession. It does not explain the census’s sin by naming pride, missing ransom payments, or another motive.
The route’s syntax and the names Tahtim-hodshi and Dan-jaan are uncertain. The draft preserves them rather than supplying a reconstructed itinerary.

The source gives eight hundred thousand fighting men in Israel, five hundred thousand men in Judah, seven years of famine as an option, and seventy thousand deaths. The endpoint “appointed time” is not further specified.
The LORD relents; David asks that the hand fall on him and his father’s house instead of the people. Both the divine action and his plea remain explicit.
The Hebrew can be read as calling Araunah “the king,” as here, or as addressing David as “O king” within Araunah’s continuing speech. His status is not explained in this account.
The price is fifty silver shekels for the threshing floor and cattle. The draft does not replace it with an amount from another account.
vocabulary: His heart struck him
An image of inward conviction, kept visible before David’s confession.
Seer
A designation for one who receives divine revelation; Gad is also called a prophet.
Threshing sledges
Agricultural tools drawn over harvested grain to separate it from the stalks.
Well-being offerings
Sacrificial offerings associated with peace or well-being before God.
